doc.title: Michael Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 22, 2021

title: Life lessons from older bandleaders on the road
summary: He learned to let travel problems roll off, and observed leaders' professionalism and audience presentation.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Thanks. That’s some very valuable insight into that mysterious and rather magical process that happens in jazz. Did you have life lessons? You talked about going on the road and how important that was with mostly people who were older than you. In your observations of them, what kind of things did you learn?

One important lesson was how they could easily let the unpredictabilities or when things like being on the road, when things go wrong, when things don’t go according to plan, how easily they could let those things roll off their back. How it didn’t bother them half as much as it was bothering me. And that was an important lesson to learn. Why are we taking a 7 a.m. flight? The gig is not until 9 o’clock at night and the flight is only an hour and a half long. Why are we having to get up to take this flight? There is eight flights that day. And I’m bitching and I’m mad and blah-blah-blah. And I look at the bandleaders, they just roll with it. So road experiences like that. Like okay, shut up. Deal with it. You know if it doesn’t bother them it shouldn’t bother you. Just yeah, professional decorum, how the bandleader presented their music to the audience, every leader has their own way of communicating with the audience, of presenting their repertoire, of engaging with the audience. All different — all these types of things you know, how they conducted themselves as bandleaders, as businessmen, as entertainers, all that kind of stuff. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
